rationale: A wins slightly because it is more disciplined about what the facts can carry. Its line "The contrarian frame collapses without the education-usage number" is the adult in the room; B's "It Won't Say How Often They Actually Work" is a sharp instinct, but it turns "not disclosed" into a quasi-refusal. A's pricing angle is thinner than it thinks, but B's best accountability angle needs the proof it admits it does not have.
gaps_in_A: "When the AI does the building, Replit charges for the work, not the seat" overstates the pricing fact; the update says usage-based pricing on top of subscriptions, not that seats stop mattering.
"whether agents break seat-based pricing" builds a market thesis from one vendor's pricing model. That needs comparison points, not just a launch.
It leaves reliability as an uncomfortable question instead of testing whether "reliability and how often generated apps work without fixes are not disclosed" can support its own accountability angle.
"Replit bets its next users will never write a line of code" is directionally fair, but "next users" and "never" need proof beyond positioning for non-engineers and vibe coders.
gaps_in_B: "It Won't Say How Often They Actually Work" and "explicitly declines to disclose reliability rates" overstate the record; the update says reliability is not disclosed, not that Replit refused to answer.
"the market has moved from AI that assists developers to AI that replaces the development workflow" turns one launch into a market conclusion before the requested comparable offerings exist.
"built its user base ... on ... explicit traction in schools" decorates "used heavily in education" into a stronger origin story than the update gives.

Rejecting "Pricing model analysis" as "no_journalist_shape" is too dismissive; usage-based pricing on top of subscriptions is a real business-of-software hook if Replit can provide tiers and sample bills.
